title: Discord 向游戏工作室推销的增长方案：哪些能力已被验证，哪些值得争取

Discord’s Growth Pitch to Game Studios: What’s Proven and What to Ask For
0
Discord’s Growth Pitch to Game Studios: What’s Proven and What to Ask For
Business
Oct 26
Written by
Michail Katkoff
Discord wants you
By
Jen Donahoe
, Strategic Marketing Consultant and Deconstructor of Fun co-host
Jen Donahoe's conversation with Jules Shumaker, Chief Business Officer at Discord, on five tools Discord is building for game studios, and why now is the time to strike a deal.
Full conversation with Jules Shumaker:
Watch on YouTube
·
Listen on Spotify
User acquisition for games keeps getting harder. Discord says it has an answer: 90 million daily and 200 million monthly users, more than 90% of whom played a game in the past month, by its own count. Jules Shumaker, Discord's Chief Business Officer, made the case to me on Deconstructor of Fun.
Let me concede the obvious first: Discord is selling. It filed confidentially for an IPO in January, and Nitro subscriptions alone make a thin public-market story. This is also its second run at games. In 2018 it added a games catalog to Nitro, then pulled it a year later because few subscribers played. Discord needs this attempt to work, and it needs studios to prove it. That makes now the time to negotiate, and it's why we're talking about it.
Discord pitches four ways it helps games grow: user acquisition, retention and engagement, monetization, and reengagement. Source: Discord.
Disclosure: Jules and I overlapped at EA and shared a boss, and I've been on Discord since 2017. I'm a fan of both, so weigh my read with that in mind.
1. Your Discord server is a launch asset if you staff it
Jules starts with where players already are. Discord's developer documentation says 66% of its users play games with friends every week, and the anniversary post counted more than 2 billion hours of gaming a month. More than 30% of games that haven't launched yet already have a Discord server, and more than 9,000 official game communities live on the platform with over 80 million members combined.
Claiming your server unlocks a game profile page, and Jules says 48 million users a day find games through player and game profiles. How many of those become installs is the number that matters, and Discord hasn't shared it. Claim the profile anyway, since it's free shelf space, and ask your Discord contact for your own profile's conversion data. Jules is flexible on who runs the server. Riot lets community members own its servers, and she counts that as a strategy in its own right.
If your audience is PC or core, a server before your first playtest is cheap insurance, as long as someone owns moderation from day one. An empty or unmoderated server is worse than none, because players read it as a signal about the game. On casual mobile, check whether your players are on Discord before you staff one.
2. Social players retain better
The Social SDK links a player's Discord friends into your game. Players send invites, jump into a friend's session, and see what friends are playing. There's no license fee, and Discord provides solution architects and developer education. Marvel Rivals and Valorant run it, and Jules named Call of Duty and Battlefield as going live.
Discord's headline number: linked players show a 31% increase in D28 retention and play 1.5 more game days a month than unlinked players. Discord's documentation adds that PC players played a median of 6 times longer when they played with at least one Discord friend.
Very rarely do you have the exact same goal as a partner, and we both do.
— Jules Shumaker
3. Discord knows who stopped playing your game
Reactivation is one of my biggest challenges as a marketer. In the data I've seen, returning players run above the median on almost every metric, especially paying, and they are the hardest group to find.
Discord users choose to share what they're playing so friends can join them. That gives Discord a signal most ad platforms lack: it knows who played your game and stopped. Among campaigns existing games buy on Discord, about half go to finding new players and half to reactivation.
Once you have that player, my goodness, hold onto them.
— Jules Shumaker
Give reactivation its own budget line and a CPA target, and run a lapsed player campaign against a holdout. This is where the IPO timing helps most: ask for test credits and a joint incrementality read. Then ask one more question before you sign. Can a competitor target players who stopped playing your game? If the answer is yes, negotiate an exclusion.
4. Rewarded ads work on Discord's payers, so test them on yours
Discord's ad business runs on opt in, rewarded formats. Quests let players play a game for a few minutes or watch a video, then collect a reward. The suite adds hero takeovers of the Quest page, a performance based Video Quest priced on outcomes like cost per install, and a self serve ad manager so studios of any size can run their own campaigns. Video Quest and the self serve ad manager are brand new, so performance data will take a few quarters to build. New ad products usually come with launch pricing and hands-on support, which lowers the cost of finding out. On mobile, Jules says ad performance runs high while reach is still low.
Discord reports 3x more positive sentiment toward its ads, and players are 71% less likely to skip or be annoyed by them, compared with traditional ads. Discord has not specified the comparison set. Source: Discord internal data, December 31, 2025.
Our payers participate in the ads at a higher rate than our non-payers.
— Jules Shumaker
Every mobile game developer can take that finding and use it right now. There's a lot of data showing players enjoy rewarded ads when they opt in and get something of value for their time, and I pay in most of my games and would happily watch a rewarded video here and there.
